description: We’re participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, tackling Abandoned but not Forgotten. We aim to combine technology, storytelling and research to bring the stories of NASA equipment left on the Moon and Mars to life. Developers, designers, researchers and storytellers are welcome to share ideas and help us build something meaningful!
summary:
Excavation 2142 is an interactive archive that helps young space enthusiasts explore NASA hardware left on the Moon and Mars. Visitors can browse 16 artifact records, four lunar and 12 Martian open evidence-linked dossiers, follow mission timelines and explore NASA-based 3D models of both worlds.

The project addresses the challenge by turning verified mission records into engaging stories about what each machine was built to do, the science it enabled and its documented status. The Detective Mode invites learners to investigate real NASA evidence and adjust their own likelihood ratings across five possible outcomes. These ratings represent the learner’s judgment, not NASA statistics.

The 2142 setting adds an imaginative frame while source links and clear labels distinguish fiction from history. This matters because hardware left behind on other worlds is part of humanity’s scientific record. Making that history accessible can spark curiosity about space exploration and show how evidence helps us understand past missions.
details:
Excavation 2142 is an interactive archive exploring NASA hardware left on the Moon and Mars. Visitors can browse 16 artifact record, four lunar and twelve Martian. Follow a mission timeline and open dossiers with mission context, images and links to NASA sources.

Detective Mode turns those same records into an evidence exercise. Learners review cited information, compare five possible artifacts and adjust each option’s likelihood from 1 to 10. Ratings begin at 5 and change only when the learner adjusts them and a final choice reveals whether the match is correct and links back to the supporting record.

The project makes mission history more approachable by showing that equipment left behind still has a story: what it was built to do, what science it enabled and what evidence remains. Its intended impact is to help school-age space enthusiasts practice comparing sources and reasoning from evidence while exploring real Moon and Mars missions.

We built it with TypeScript, React, Vite and Three.js, with artifact and case data stored in separate JSON files. The archive meaningfully uses NASA’s NSSDCA Master Catalog for catalog IDs, mission details and documented hardware status, alongside NASA mission records and credited NASA images.

The creative framing imagines future archaeologists studying the space age in 2142. That setting shapes the interface and storytelling, while historical claims and data remain clearly tied to NASA records. We considered accuracy, clear sourcing, age-appropriate learning and keeping fictional presentation separate from historical evidence.
